text.p: European consortium Airbus Industrie said on Sunday it has launched a corporate jet version of its A319 narrow-body aircraft, rivalling a business plane being sold by U.S. competitor Boeing.
Investment for the new product will be around $30 million, Airbus managing director Jean Pierson told a news conference on the second day of the Paris air show.

Airbus's corporate jet will compete with archrival Boeing Co's 737-700 Business Jet, which was shown off in colourful livery at the air show on Saturday. The U.S. firm sold two Business Jets last week, priced at $30.5 million apiece before fitting out, taking its total orders to 20 aircraft from 18 customers since its launch last year.

The Airbus A319CJ will be available in early 1999 and will have the "widest and most flexible interior of all the competing business jet types" the company said in a statement. It will fly between eight and 50 passengers, and will have a range of 11,600 nautical miles (11,600 km).

The Airbus and Boeing products will come at the top end of the corporate jet business which has up to now been the preserve of U.S. Gulfstream, which is aggressively marketing its sleek new Gulfstream V, and rival Canadian firm Bombardier BBD.TO, which offers its Global Express long-range jets.
Boeing said buyers so far for its Business Jet include blue-chip Fortune 100 companies, heads of state and wealthy individuals, such as champion golfer Greg Norman, who signed up last week.
As a result, Boeing has decided to produce nine of the aircraft next year instead of the four originally planned, and 24 aircraft in 1999, up from the six to eight previously planned.
Airbus is a consortium composed of French state-owned Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (Casa) of Spain.
